title: Getting a songwriter a publishing contract
summary: Matassa explains how his name came to be on a song: the writer had no contract, so he arranged one (Hill and Range, he thinks) and his widow still collects; Wexler is mentioned.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Yeah, because usually you went in the studio and you did a couple, you did more than two sides. Oh, yeah. We generally did four sides. Four sides a session. Yeah. So, well, now that I've gotten here and we're talking about songwriter credits, I mean, I noticed your name on some other tunes. This is one. Yeah. One more song really interesting. Yeah. Yeah. How did you get, how did you get, how did your name get on that? I really exactly put that one together. How did your name get on that? And what happened was he didn't have a songwriter's contract.
And so, I said, well, you know, we need to organize all of this stuff and do something. And that's what we did. And I got him a contract with Hill and Range, I think.
I think it was Hill and Range.

I don't know. It's been so long. But I think it was Hill and Range. And I never did it. And I never did it. I never did it. Whatever money there was. And then he had it. And then his widow, I presume, still gets it.
Oh, yeah, yeah. They're sorting all that out right now through the estate. But Jerry Wexler, when they did it, Jerry didn't ask for? No. Usually they ask for the publishing. I understand.
But you've got to understand the song existed before he did it. Before he recorded it.
And he did, and also he did, what was the thing Fast Downbone did? Marty Grudin. Marty Grudin.
He didn't have a contract on that either. And I got him a contract on that either. Mm-hmm. Because he wasn't going to. You know, he was on of my getting money off the Fast Downbone.
